The step counts are plausible: about 315 steps per ring, less gates and breaches. Two corrections. (1) The "field furrow hatching" is really a sage rectangle with a few cross-grid lines ("outlying gridded fields", 2-4 fields of roughly 10 lines each). That is cheap and fits vectors or a pattern fill. It is not heavy texture. (2) The coast and river rims should not simply stay raster in a vector city. Their outline should come from the same atlas-sampled mask (sampleCityMask), traced once into shared vertices with the atlas coast and rivers, because that outline is the registration-bearing part. Only the soft ink halo is texture. So: merge the wall into runs (one path per unbroken run between gates and breaches). Keep stipple, scrub, snow and the vignette as raster or pattern fills (a vignette can be an SVG mask or the canvas layer under the vectors). Do not port draw calls one for one. The arithmetic checks out: 9000/767 = 11.734 m per grid cell, times 768/800 = 11.265 m per atlas px, not 11.25. Composing with gridToWorld gives gridX = (x/9000 + 0.5)*767 and atlasX = 1060 + gridX*800/768, as claimed. A grep of index.html finds 1060 and 1240 only in that comment (plus base64 data), so no function does the atlas conversion. Settlements are placed through gridToWorld(s.gridX) with no atlas-pixel step. The "only holds for seed epeshu" point is also right: the frame comes from CUSTOM_MAP_DATA, and procedural seeds have no atlas window.

votes.corrected: REGISTRATION, sim-to-atlas only. A vector city layer in the atlas is authored in atlas px and needs no sim transform at all. items.summary: A shared atlas/sim city geometry needs one coded transform, shared atlas-derived inputs, a keyed per-city stream and registered canon input; the registration parts alone fix the atlas in either medium, and the whole-world fingerprint effect is an inference.

prior_record.claim: A shared city geometry (one generator, rendered as 2D vector in the atlas and 3D in the sim) would require the following. (a) One coded atlas-px ↔ sim-metre transform (S1) in both apps. (b) Shared inputs as well as shared code: one land/water mask (atlas-derived), one road-entry source (atlas traced roads rather than the sim's 192² A*), one river source, one footprint radius, and fixed settlement positions (fix Shengo and Rhup). The same code fed different inputs still diverges. (c) A per-city keyed stream, e.g. xmur3(seed+':city:'+name), instead of the sequential W.rng.gen. Moving planStreetsFor off the global stream shifts every later W.rng.gen draw, which changes the whole epeshu world and its determinism fingerprint. (d) For Epēshu, canon input: the DM chart warped to the atlas by control points (atlas wins), with its streets, quays and POIs digitised into that frame. Otherwise the generator only reproduces invented streets (S4). (e) A medium that serialises plain polylines and polygons (streets {pts,w}, parcels, wall, gates, bridges) in atlas px or metres, which both a Leaflet vector or canvas painter and the three.js ribbon builder can consume. (f) Coordination: genCityCanvas and sampleCityMask are pinned by source hash in the mobile track, so replacing them is a mobile re-pin. Filigree slice C owns the painted city look (R4 never label blocks, R7 nothing at rest). Moving Epēshu's labels or streets moves street fixture focuses, so Street 1 must re-freeze (Street 1→3 re-run).

prior_record.applies_to_us_proposed: Both. Items (a), (b) and (d) are REGISTRATION, and they fix the misalignment whichever medium is used. Items (c) and (e) are MEDIUM, and they give crisp, interactive, shared vertices. Done the other way round (vector first, still placed by cityBox), the result misaligns exactly like today's raster.

(1) expression_name.values.zoom: "in style layout and paint properties, [\"zoom\"] may only appear as the input to a top-level \"step\" or \"interpolate\" expression." (2) layer.minzoom: "At zoom levels less than the minzoom, the layer will be hidden." layer.maxzoom (not cited): hidden at zoom >= maxzoom. (3) source_vector.maxzoom: "Maximum zoom level for which tiles are available... Data from tiles at the maxzoom are used when displaying the map at higher zoom levels." Narrowest supported claim: a style's zoom-dependent paint/layout values must be a top-level step (stepwise) or interpolate (continuous in fractional zoom, e.g. linear/exponential), layers can be hard-gated with minzoom/maxzoom, and a vector source's maxzoom makes deeper zooms reuse the maxzoom tiles' data. The claim overreaches in two places: it calls step/interpolate outputs 'continuous' (step is not), and it asserts crisp re-rasterization versus pixel stretching, which no cited quote states. The core spec facts hold, so the severity is minor.

votes.corrected: [medium] Partly, with corrections. (1) No style interpolation in Leaflet 1.9.4 (docs/research/cartographic-filigree.md: "Not in Leaflet. It must be hand-driven from the zoom event"). The equivalent is a pure function of fractional zoom, in the same shape as baseOpacity(z)/overlayOpacity(z), run from worldOpacityUpdate on map.on('zoom zoomend moveend'). The filigree note's own recipe is to write one CSS var --z on 'zoom' and have the ink use calc(). That fits the mobile per-frame budget better than calling setStyle on many L.Path objects on every zoom event. Also, during Leaflet's animated zoom the SVG/canvas renderer is CSS-scaled and only redrawn at zoomend, so stroke-width writes made mid-animation are mostly not seen. (2) Hard minzoom/maxzoom gates already exist in hand-made form: the opacity ramps, the map-tier-d and show-uncharted class toggles, and add/remove in worldCityUpdate. Each pane or layer can be gated the same way, with no new machinery. (3) "Overzoom" has no direct Leaflet counterpart. L.Path geometry in CRS.Simple is re-projected at every zoom and so is crisp at any zoom with no tile source. maxNativeZoom only covers raster tiles (the base is already overzoomed from z5 to Z_STREET 11.5). So the crispness gain comes only from city geometry authored as vectors in atlas world px, and it stays a medium, rendering-only benefit. It fixes nothing about registration: a vector city placed through cityBox/FOOT_R misaligns exactly as the raster does. Alignment needs anchor and control points tied to atlas features (coast, rivers, roads), with the art bent to the atlas. Any vector city layer must sit beside the pinned genCityCanvas/washMake/sampleCityMask (UG3 atlas_fn_sha, cityCanvasSha) and leave them unchanged. It must stay seeded and deterministic, wait for the mid-flight mobile atlas lane (Mobile 5-9), and respect filigree slice C plus R4/R7 (no block labels, nothing at rest).
votes.reason: The main assessment checks out against HEAD. maps-site/index.html has Leaflet with zoomSnap:0, baseOpacity(z) and overlayOpacity(z) as piecewise-linear ramps, and worldOpacityUpdate on map.on('zoom zoomend moveend', ...). The base layer uses maxNativeZoom with maxZoom:Z_STREET and Z_STREET=11.5. cartographic-filigree.md confirms there is no style interpolation in Leaflet. The point that crispness does not fix registration is correct. Three refinements change what acting on it should look like. First, writing stroke per frame per path is the wrong mechanism for the mobile budget; filigree already prescribes one CSS --z var with calc() ink, and Leaflet CSS-scales vectors during zoom animation anyway. Second, MapLibre's "source maxzoom overzoom" does not transfer as a concept. Leaflet vectors are untiled, re-projected geometry that is crisp at every zoom, so the real precondition is authoring city geometry as vectors registered to atlas features, not building a tile or overzoom pipeline. Third, the claim does not mention the pinned-hash, mobile-lane and filigree slice C/R4/R7 constraints that any vector city layer must respect.

items.summary: OSM vector ladders show merged blocks at low zoom and footprints later with a fade band (the OSM Bright sub-claim slightly overreaches); transferable as a medium LOD shape only, not an alignment fix.

prior_record.claim: [medium] Buildings are generalized by zoom in the OSM vector ladder. OpenMapTiles serves merged building blocks at z13 (DBSCAN-clustered, buffer-unioned, VW-simplified) and individual polygons from z14. OSM Bright fades building fill and opacity across z13-16 and offsets a 'building-top' fill for a pseudo-3D look. MapLibre's 3D-buildings example starts extrusions at minzoom 15 and interpolates height from 0 at z15 to full at z16. OSM Carto draws buildings from z14 and drops any smaller than one pixel.
prior_record.applies_to_us_proposed: [medium] Yes as a ladder shape: wards/blocks as merged fills first, individual buildings later, with a fade band. In our zoom space the base fades over z6.2-8 and the overlay over z6.8-7.8. Today genCityCanvas paints everything at once at 2048 px. A vector city would need the same banding (block hulls, then footprints past roughly z8.5-9), which also limits how many paths exist during the descent. The z-values are ours to choose, and the ladder must respect R7 (nothing at rest) and R4 (no block labels).

evidence.quote: label="layer_building | <z13> z13 | <z14_> z14+ "
ST_ClusterDBSCAN(o.geometry, eps := zres14, minpoints := 1) ... geometry := ST_SimplifyVW(geometry, zres14vw);
'type': 'fill-extrusion', 'minzoom': 15, ... 'fill-extrusion-height': ['interpolate', ['linear'], ['zoom'], 15, 0, 16, ['get', 'render_height']]
AND way_area > 1*!pixel_width!::real*!pixel_height!::real ... properties: minzoom: 14

votes.corrected: All five sources were fetched and the quotes are present. Four of the five sub-claims hold as stated. The OSM Bright sub-claim overreaches slightly. Narrowest supported claim: (1) OpenMapTiles layer_building serves merged blocks only at zoom_level = 13 and individual polygons from z14 up. The blocks are DBSCAN-clustered (eps = Zres(14)), buffer-unioned, have small holes and small blocks removed, and are simplified with ST_SimplifyVW. (2) In OSM Bright's style.json, the 'building-top' layer's fill-opacity runs from 0 at z13 to 1 at z16, and its fill-translate runs from [0,0] at z14 to [-2,-2] at z16. The base 'building' layer has no opacity stops, only a fill-color change from #f2eae2 to #dfdbd7 across z15.5-16. The 'pseudo-3D look' is a reasonable reading of the offset top layer but is not stated in the style. (3) The MapLibre 3D-buildings example uses a fill-extrusion layer with minzoom 15, and height is interpolated from 0 at z15 to render_height at z16. (4) OSM Carto's buildings layer has minzoom 14 and filters on way_area > 1 pixel_width * pixel_height, so it drops buildings smaller than one pixel at the rendered zoom.
votes.reason:
Checked by fetching each raw GitHub file.

Confirmed:
- building.sql line 2 contains the etldoc label '<z13> z13 | <z14_> z14+'. The z13 branch reads osm_building_block_gen_z13 WHERE zoom_level = 13. The polygon branch reads WHERE zoom_level >= 14.
- update_building.sql contains ST_ClusterDBSCAN(... eps := zres14, minpoints := 1), the ST_Buffer/ST_Union/ST_Buffer mitre union, and geometry := ST_SimplifyVW(geometry, zres14vw). The quote joins the two lines with '...', which is fair.

Registration (fitting the plan to the atlas coast, rivers and roads) has to be solved first, and on its own terms. So "footprints from about z8.5-9" would leave a raster capital less than one zoom of footprint range. A vector layer is what would let the band reach Z_STREET 11.5. The ladder must be seeded (xmur3/mulberry32), with no Math.random. (2) Epēshu and Summarch stay the DM's raster chart art. It never says that banding is about rendering and density and does nothing for the anchoring the owner asked about. It misses that cityMaxZ (about z9.3 for a procedural capital) leaves the proposed z8.5-9 footprint band almost no room unless the city becomes vector. It doesn't exclude the canon DM charts (Epēshu by B-33) or keep the pinned genCityCanvas untouched. It doesn't hand the thresholds to filigree, which already measured the z8.3-9.3 textile band and owns F3-D city grain. The pseudo-3D and extrusion parts belong to the living and street tracks, not the atlas sheet.

items.summary: Vector tiles carry no frame of their own (tile-local integer extent, 4096 only an example), so any local-frame city plan must be transformed into atlas px before drawing.

prior_record.claim: [registration] Vector tiles carry no frame of their own. Geometry is integer coordinates in a tile-local extent (typically 4096), and the decoder must already know the tile's bounds and projection. The spec explicitly allows any projection and tiling scheme.
prior_record.applies_to_us_proposed: [registration] Yes, as a principle. Vectors only line up because everyone agrees on one frame before encoding. A city plan authored in its own local frame (like MFCG, or genCityCanvas's 2048 canvas) must be transformed into atlas world px (CRS.Simple, NZ=4) before any layer draws it. Picking 'vector' gives no alignment for free.

evidence.quote: A Vector Tile SHOULD NOT contain information about its bounds and projection. The file format assumes that the decoder knows the bounds and projection of a Vector Tile before decoding it.
Vector Tiles MAY be used to represent data with any projection and tile extent scheme.

votes.corrected: Holds, with one softening: the spec says extent 4096 is an example ("if a tile has an extent of 4096..."), not a typical or required value. The spec requires an integer `extent` per layer; "typically 4096" is conventional, not spec text. The second quote says "any projection and tile extent scheme", which the claim paraphrases as "tiling scheme". The "applies_to_us" repo facts check out: genCityCanvas uses GEN_SIZE=2048, and NZ=4 is set in maps-site/index.html.
votes.reason: I fetched the raw mapbox vector-tile-spec 2.1 README. Both quotes appear verbatim: "A Vector Tile SHOULD NOT contain information about its bounds and projection. The file format assumes that the decoder knows the bounds and projection of a Vector Tile before decoding it." and "Vector Tiles MAY be used to represent data with any projection and tile extent scheme." Section 4.3 also says a layer MUST contain an integer `extent`, with 4096 as the worked example. The claim's "no frame of its own" and "decoder must already know bounds and projection" match the first quote. The only overreach is the wording "typically 4096" and the loose paraphrase of "tile extent scheme" as "tiling scheme".

votes.corrected: [registration] Yes, as a principle; the MVT format itself (protobuf tiles, 4096 extent, decoder) does not transfer. A single no-build file has no decoder and no tile server, and nothing here needs one. The transferable lesson is that geometry lines up only when every layer agrees on one frame before it is drawn. The atlas already has that frame: atlas world px at NZ=4, reached through px(x,y) = map.unproject([x,y],NZ) in maps-site/index.html. The roads, lanes and routes drawn with L.polyline/L.polygon already go through it. A city plan authored in its own local frame (MFCG, or genCityCanvas's GEN_SIZE=2048 canvas) must be transformed into atlas world px before any layer draws it. Today that transform is cityBox(a,w,h): a box centred on the anchor, half-size FOOT_R[kind], scaled to the image aspect. A capital's 2048 canvas spans about 52 world px. cityBox is a placement guess, not a registration. Choosing vector over raster gives no alignment for free: polylines sent through the same cityBox transform misalign exactly as the image does. The fix is a per-city transform fitted to atlas features (coast and river from sampleCityMask, road endpoints from buildCityStubs, or control points picked on the DM art), applied to the plan's coordinates. The art bends to the atlas, never the reverse. Rendering medium remains a separate decision.
votes.reason: The quoted spec text is accurate, and the stated principle matches the code. cityBox in maps-site/index.html centres any image or plan on the anchor using only FOOT_R[kind] and the image aspect. GEN_SIZE=2048 is the plan's local frame. px() / map.unproject(...,NZ) is the shared world frame that the existing vector overlays already use. So the applies_to_us verdict is right and acting on it is correct, because it keeps registration and rendering medium separate. The correction only (a) drops any suggestion of adopting MVT tiles or a decoder, which would break the no-build single-file rule and is unnecessary, (b) names the existing px() frame and identifies cityBox as the transform to replace, and (c) points to the deterministic, seed-pure inputs (sampleCityMask, buildCityStubs) for fitting the transform without moving the atlas. Any change to genCityCanvas or sampleCityMask themselves must respect the mobile track's source-hash pins (atlas_fn_sha and cityCanvasSha). Fitting a transform outside those functions avoids disturbing them.

items.summary: geojson-vt and Leaflet.VectorGrid (last release 1.3.0, 2017) can tile vectors in-browser, but adding them breaks the vendored-Leaflet-only pin (SRI attribute plus SHA256SUMS); a hand-rolled simplifier suffices.

prior_record.claim: [medium] In-browser tiling is possible without a build step. geojson-vt slices GeoJSON into vector tiles on the fly and simplifies per zoom (tolerance 3, extent 4096). Leaflet.VectorGrid's Slicer draws those tiles in Leaflet 1.x as SVG or Canvas. VectorGrid's latest npm release is 1.3.0, published 2017-08-28.
prior_record.applies_to_us_proposed: [medium] Probably not as a dependency. The atlas vendors only Leaflet (maps-site/vendor/leaflet@1.9.4, pinned by SRI in SHA256SUMS), and VectorGrid is unmaintained since 2017. One city holds hundreds to low thousands of polygons in a footprint of about 50 world px, so a hand-rolled per-band simplification (Leaflet's own LineUtil.simplify, or precomputed block hulls) in one file covers the need. Tiling only pays off for atlas-wide vector layers.

evidence.quote: A highly efficient JavaScript library for slicing GeoJSON data into vector tiles on the fly ... the tiles are simplified, retaining the minimum level of detail appropriate for each zoom level
L.VectorGrid.Slicer for displaying GeoJSON or TopoJSON data ... VectorGrid leverages the GridLayer feature introduced in Leaflet 1.0.0.

votes.corrected: Claim holds as stated. Two attribution notes. The "SVG or Canvas" rendering is not in the cited VectorGrid README quote. It is in the Leaflet.VectorGrid.js source, where the default is `rendererFactory: L.svg.tile`; the Canvas option is inferred from the option name and from the README's TODO list ("Offscreen canvases in Canvas"), not read in the source. The "tolerance 3, extent 4096" values are the geojson-vt default options (README options block), not something the quoted sentence says.
votes.reason: I fetched all three sources and confirmed the quotes. The geojson-vt README says it slices "GeoJSON data into vector tiles on the fly" "on the browser side (without a server)". It says tiles are "simplified, retaining the minimum level of detail appropriate for each zoom level". Its default options are tolerance 3 and extent 4096. The README also gives a browser script tag (unpkg), so no build step is needed. The VectorGrid README lists "L.VectorGrid.Slicer for displaying GeoJSON or TopoJSON data" and says it "leverages the GridLayer feature introduced in Leaflet 1.0.0". Its install notes show a bundled unpkg script that includes geojson-vt, and `Leaflet.VectorGrid.js` expects a global `geojsonvt`. The npm registry shows dist-tags latest = 1.3.0 and time["1.3.0"] = 2017-08-28T06:31:31.276Z. The package's metadata "modified" stamp is 2022-06-19, but that is registry metadata and not a release. On applies_to_us, `maps-site/vendor/SHA256SUMS` pins leaflet@1.9.4 files (dist/leaflet.js, leaflet.css, images, LICENSE) and `maps-site/vendor` holds only `leaflet@1.9.4` and `fonts`, so "vendors only Leaflet" is correct. "Unmaintained since 2017" is an inference from the last release date, and the registry does not state it. unpkg could not be reached from here (the proxy returned 403 on the CONNECT), so the existence of the bundled file is taken from the README only.

votes.corrected: [medium] Not as a dependency. Two small corrections. First, the vendored Leaflet (maps-site/vendor/leaflet@1.9.4) is pinned in two places: by an SRI integrity attribute on its <script src="vendor/leaflet@1.9.4/dist/leaflet.js"> tag in maps-site/index.html, and separately by maps-site/vendor/SHA256SUMS. SHA256SUMS is not itself the SRI. Adding geojson-vt and VectorGrid (unmaintained since the 1.3.0 release on 2017-08-28) would mean new vendored files, new pins and a new risk surface for very little gain. Second, the per-band simplification does not need to be hand-rolled. With L.canvas()/L.svg, Leaflet 1.9.4's own L.Polyline/L.Polygon already re-project on zoom and simplify in screen pixels through smoothFactor (L.LineUtil.simplify), and they clip to the view. Precomputed per-band block hulls are worth having only where generalisation has to be cartographic (R4: never label blocks) and not just geometric. City scale is small: FOOT_R in maps-site/index.html is capital 26 / town 14 / village 9 / ruin 8 world px, so a city spans about 16-52 px across and holds hundreds to low thousands of polygons. One canvas renderer per active city is enough for that, and tiling would only pay off for atlas-wide vector layers. Neither tiling nor simplification affects registration. A vector city placed through cityBox misaligns exactly as the raster does, so the alignment fix lives in the anchor and transform data, not in the choice of renderer. Any new vector city code must be seeded and deterministic. It sits beside the hash-pinned genCityCanvas/sampleCityMask (UG3 atlas_fn_sha, cityCanvasSha) and must not alter them, and it waits for the Mobile 5-9 atlas lane to land.
votes.reason: The library facts are plausible and match the cited READMEs and npm metadata. The verdict (do not adopt VectorGrid/geojson-vt, keep it to one file) is right for a single vanilla file with no build and vendored, hash-pinned Leaflet. I checked the HEAD export. maps-site/vendor holds only leaflet@1.9.4 and fonts. SHA256SUMS lists the leaflet files, and the script tag has its own sha256 integrity attribute, so "pinned by SRI in SHA256SUMS" mixes up two separate mechanisms. FOOT_R={capital:26,town:14,village:9,ruin:8} confirms that "about 50 world px" holds only for capitals. The claim also leaves out that Leaflet vector paths already simplify per zoom through smoothFactor and clipping, so a hand-rolled LineUtil.simplify pass is mostly redundant. It also never says that the renderer and tiling are separate from registration, which is what actually causes the shift the owner complains about. These are gaps in precision, not a wrong conclusion, so the claim holds with a corrected applies_to_us.

items.summary: During a flyTo, Leaflet vector content is a CSS-scaled copy of its last frame redrawn only at moveend (flyTo never sets _animatingZoom), so a vector city looks worse than the raster mid-descent unless hidden or redrawn.

prior_record.claim: [medium] How Leaflet 1.9.4 vectors behave during zoom (from the source). The Renderer listens to 'zoom' and 'zoomanim' and only CSS-transforms its container (_updateTransform). Paths are re-projected at zoomend, and Canvas._update returns early while _animatingZoom. flyTo's frame() calls _move() every rAF, which fires 'zoom'. So during a flyTo, vector content is a CSS-scaled copy of the last drawn state until moveend, clipped to the renderer's padding (default 0.1 of the view). Inference, not a quote: a Canvas city would blur under the 2^dz scale and SVG stroke widths would grow and then snap at moveend; on zoom-out, content beyond the padding is missing until moveend.
prior_record.applies_to_us_proposed: [medium] Yes, and it matters for flyIntoCity/ensureArrival, which fly several zoom levels in one animation (target max(z, cityMaxZ-0.5), roughly z9.4-10.3 for current plans). A vector city that crossfades in during the descent (the way ensureCityOverlay adds the overlay eagerly) would look worse mid-fly than the raster overlay, which resizes exactly each frame. Mitigations: keep the raster as the in-flight surface and reveal vectors after moveend, or own a custom layer that redraws on 'zoom' within the per-frame budget. Both are the living-chart track's call (H2z zoom-through).

evidence.quote: viewreset: this._reset, zoom: this._onZoom, moveend: this._update, zoomend: this._onZoomEnd
_onZoomEnd: function () { for (var id in this._layers) { this._layers[id]._project(); } }
_update: function () { if (this._map._animatingZoom && this._bounds) { return; }
this._move( this.unproject(from.add(to.subtract(from).multiplyBy(u(s) / u1)), startZoom), this.getScaleZoom(w0 / w(s), startZoom), {flyTo: true});
// @option padding: Number = 0.1 // How much to extend the clip area around the map view

votes.corrected: Holds as written. One precision to add: the Canvas._update early-return on _animatingZoom is real but concerns wheel/pinch/setZoom animations; flyTo never sets _animatingZoom (it only calls _move), so for a flyTo the operative facts are zoom to _onZoom to CSS transform, with redraw only at moveend (_update, plus zoomend to _project). Narrowest form: during a flyTo, a vector renderer's content is a CSS-scaled copy of its last drawn state, clipped to the padded container, until the final _moveEnd.
votes.reason: I fetched the Leaflet v1.9.4 source and confirmed every quote (whitespace and line breaks aside). Renderer.js getEvents has viewreset: _reset, zoom: _onZoom, moveend: _update, zoomend: _onZoomEnd. It adds zoomanim: _onAnimZoom when zoom-animated, and both handlers call _updateTransform, which applies DomUtil.setTransform(container, offset, scale) with scale = getZoomScale(zoom, this._zoom). _onZoomEnd only calls _project() on each layer, and padding is 0.1 ("How much to extend the clip area around the map view"). The _update that sizes the container to the padded bounds and fires 'update' (which redraws) runs only on moveend or viewreset. Canvas._update has `if (this._map._animatingZoom && this._bounds) { return; }`. Map.flyTo frame() calls this._move(unproject(...), getScaleZoom(w0 / w(s), startZoom), {flyTo: true}) each rAF, and _move fires 'zoom' whenever the zoom changed. Only the final frame calls _move(...)._moveEnd(true), which fires zoomend and then moveend. The inferences (Canvas blur, SVG stroke growth then snap, missing content beyond padding on zoom-out) follow from this and are labelled as inference. The applies_to_us section matches the repo (maps-site/index.html at HEAD). flyIntoCity calls ensureCityOverlay(key) with the comment "eager: fades in DURING the descent", sets target = Math.max(map.getZoom(), cz-0.5), and calls map.flyTo(dest,target,{duration:1.4,...}). ensureArrival is armed as a safety net. cityMaxZ = min(Z_STREET, NZ+log2(mx/(2*r))), which gives about 9.9 for Epeshu (target about 9.4) and about 10.8 for Summarch (target about 10.3) if Summarch is a town (footprint radius 14), so the stated z9.4-10.3 range holds for the two drawn plans. I did not recompute the procedural plans, so "current plans" is approximate. ImageOverlay resizing each frame on 'zoom' (_reset) is from Leaflet knowledge, not fetched, but standard for 1.9.4. The H2z zoom-through is owned by the living-chart track (docs/living/README.md).

votes.corrected: [medium] Yes, but only as a RENDERING-MEDIUM finding. It does nothing for REGISTRATION: a vector city placed through cityBox misaligns exactly as the raster does. The map is built with L.map({crs:L.CRS.Simple, zoomSnap:0, fadeAnimation:true}) and no preferCanvas, so vectors go through the default SVG renderer, one per pane. flyIntoCity flies from the current zoom to target=max(z, cityMaxZ-0.5). For the current plans that is about z9.4 for Epēshu (capital, 2863x3072), 10.3 for Summarch (town, 3072 wide), 9.7 for a 2048 procedural town, 10.3 for a village and 10.5 for a ruin, so the range is about 9.4-10.5, not 9.4-10.3. One flight often spans 4-7 levels, up to about a 2^6 CSS scale. ensureCityOverlay is called eagerly before the fly, so any vectors it adds are drawn once at the START zoom and then CSS-scaled for the whole flight until moveend. That is worse than "the last drawn state". This already happens today: buildCityStubs adds SVG L.polylines (weights 6 and 2.6, opacity .5/.6, not faded) to pane pCity inside ensureCityOverlay, so their strokes balloon during flyIntoCity and snap at moveend. L.imageOverlay listens to 'zoom' and calls _reset, which re-lays out its bounds every frame. So the raster stays exactly placed in flight and only gets softer. ensureArrival's setView(animate:false) fallback fires moveend, which redraws everything at once. Mitigations: keep the raster as the in-flight surface and add or reveal city vectors (stubs included) only after moveend, or at a zoom near the target. This also fits R7 "nothing at rest". Or write a custom layer that redraws on 'zoom' within the mobile per-frame budget. The zoom-through is the living-chart track's call (H2z), and the city look is filigree slice C's. Either way, no gen-code or pinned-hash change is needed (genCityCanvas/washMake/sampleCityMask stay untouched).
votes.reason: I checked against maps-site/index.html at HEAD. The map uses the default SVG renderer (no preferCanvas/L.canvas). flyIntoCity calls ensureCityOverlay(key) eagerly ("fades in DURING the descent"), then requestAnimationFrame(map.flyTo(dest,target,{duration:1.4})), with target=Math.max(map.getZoom(),cz-0.5) and cityMaxZ=min(Z_STREET,NZ+log2(mx/(2*FOOT_R))). That gives about 9.4 (Epēshu) to 10.5 (ruins), so the claimed 9.4-10.3 understates the top end slightly. In Leaflet 1.9.4, flyTo's frame() calls _move, which fires 'zoom' but not moveend. The Renderer only transforms its container on 'zoom' and redraws on moveend. ImageOverlay._reset runs on 'zoom', so the raster stays exact each frame, as the claim says. The inference also understates the effect: vectors added before the fly are drawn at the start zoom, not a recent one. It is already visible in the current code, because buildCityStubs puts SVG polylines in pCity during the eager ensureCityOverlay. The claim correctly hands the decision to living-chart H2z. items.summary: UG3 pins xmur3, mulberry32, genCityCanvas, washMake and sampleCityMask by source and cityCanvasSha per DPR class (the operative check, not all five profiles); a vector plan hashed as geometry removes the DPR leak but must use a sibling stream.

But it must not edit genCityCanvas or draw from its xmur3/mulberry32 stream, or the pinned hashes change. It must use a separate derived stream, or derive geometry by a pure function from the existing plan's parameters. To verify: geometry sha versus canvas-bytes sha in the planning stage.

A vector city placed through cityBox misaligns just as the raster does, and hashing it fixes nothing about alignment. (1) What the gate really checks: the gates.md text asks for equality across all five profiles, but tools/mobile-capture.js (the UG3.atlas.cityCanvasSha check) and README line 286 only require equality within each DPR class (dpr>1 versus the 1x desktop), plus equality to B0 per profile. The 1x leak is a known, accepted exception, not a live gate failure. (2) There is no shared stream to protect. genCityCanvas builds a fresh R=mulberry32(xmur3(name)()) on every call, so a vector layer that seeds its own mulberry32(xmur3(name+'|vec')()) cannot disturb it. The only real constraint is to leave the source of xmur3, mulberry32, genCityCanvas, washMake and sampleCityMask unedited (UG3 atlas_fn_sha). (3) The cleanest pure derivation without editing the pinned code is to build vector geometry from what genCityCanvas already returns (gen.stubs, gen.pois, w/h) plus its own derived stream. (5) A geometry sha (coordinates rounded to fixed precision) would be a NEW metric added to the pinned tool tools/mobile-capture.js by the central session, not a swap for cityCanvasSha. (b) The warning about not drawing from genCityCanvas's stream is moot, because each call seeds a fresh closure from xmur3(name). The real pin is the function source hashes. (c) cityCanvasSha is the sha of the cityReg 'invented' data: URLs. Swapping the raster overlay for a vector one would turn it null and fail UG3, so the raster registration must stay or the gate must be changed centrally. (d) A geometry sha needs a change to the pinned capture tool, done centrally. It is an extra metric, not a replacement. (e) genCityCanvas decides things from getImageData masks, so a 'pure function of the plan's parameters' must avoid those readbacks to be truly free of DPR. (f) Getting full geometry out of genCityCanvas edits pinned code, so it waits for the Mobile atlas lane to close and a B0 rebaseline. None of this bears on misalignment: that is a REGISTRATION problem (cityBox centred on the anchor with FOOT_R), and determinism hashing does not touch it.

items.summary: Only the coast of invented coastal plans with drawWater and mask water is registered by construction; streets, walls, rivers and gates are seeded or bearing-only.

The only drift left is Math.round on the patch origin (up to 0.25 atlas px) plus the 0.5-atlas-px resolution of the z5 mask. So constraint-based generation is the path we already have. What it lacks is a vector emitter, not better registration.
prior_record.applies_to_us_proposed: Yes. Any vector city should keep this frame: build geometry in atlas px from the same mask and approaches, then draw. MEDIUM: switching to vectors adds crispness and lets roads share vertices, but registration here is already as good as the z5 mask allows.

The mask therefore registers to the atlas coast to within the z5 mask resolution, 0.5 atlas px. The Math.round on the patch origin is NOT a drift source: the draw subtracts the rounded MK.ox/MK.oy from the exact (a.atlasX-rW)*2 coordinate, so the rounding is compensated. Land-gate bearings come from route/way polylines crossing a 2.5*footR(kind) circle (cityApproaches). That sets bearing only: the gates are placed at radius gr around a core centre that is shifted off the anchor by 7% of the canvas side when water is drawn, not where the roads cross the box edge (r). A curved road's bearing at 2.5r need not match its crossing at r, so road registration is not exact by construction. Inland cities (no mask water) have no coast registration at all. 'Constraint-based generation is the path we already have; the missing piece is a vector emitter' is a fair reading, but 'registration is already as good as the z5 mask allows' is not shown.

(2) 'Anchored by construction' covers only the coast, and only for cities whose patch holds sea. Gate bearings sampled at 2.5r are not geometry registered at the cityBox edge, and the city core is deliberately offset from the anchor when water is drawn. The 0.5 atlas px mask resolution is the right residual for the coast; the roads carry extra, unquantified error.

Everything else in an invented plan is placed by the seed or only by bearing, not registered to the atlas. (1) Rivers are seeded. In the RV block of genCityCanvas, the flow angle is R()*Math.PI*2 for 'through' rivers and only biased toward the sea for 'beside' rivers, so a plan's river does not follow the atlas river. The atlas-coordinate stubs then run out radially to 1.18r. A road that is not radial between 1.18r and 2.5r therefore ends up off the atlas line. (3) When the mask holds no water, or the side comes from t.sea, the coast falls back to the synthetic compass shoreline (shoreOff). (4) The owner's main complaint is the DM-drawn canon overlays (overlay-Epeshu, overlay-Summarch). These are placed by cityBox alone, centred on the dot and scaled from FOOT_R with no control points, and nothing in this claim fixes them. Acting on it: keep the mask and atlas-px frame for any vector emitter (the medium). But do not call registration solved. Before or alongside vectorising: trace the approach polylines from the 2.5r crossing all the way in to the gate, take river geometry from atlas data rather than the seed, and give the canon art a control-point warp onto atlas features (art bends to the atlas). Any of these changes to genCityCanvas will alter cityCanvasSha and the mobile pins, so they must be sequenced with Mobile 5-9. A vector city placed through the same cityBox inherits these same offsets.

items.summary: The two canon charts are placed by cityBox with no regard to content (no rotation, scale fit or feature fit), and L.svgOverlay is placed the same way, so the fix is content-aware registration applied to either medium.

prior_record.claim: REGISTRATION (code): the two canon cities skip registration entirely. registerCityOverlay hands Epēshu (2863x3072) and Summarch (3072x2859) to cityBox, which centres the image on the anchor dot and aspect-fits it into a 2r box (capital r=26, town r=14). The image content plays no part: no rotation, no scale fit, no fit to the atlas coast, river or roads. This is where the owner's 'doesn't perfectly anchor' comes from. A vector tracing of the same art, placed through the same cityBox (or through L.svgOverlay, which is placed the same way), would misalign identically.

items.summary: Measured on Summarch's own scale bar, the canon art and its cityBox footprint differ in scale by roughly 10-16× (assuming a 1-1.6 km Cyrikon mile; Epēshu only inferred), so registration of the insets can only be symbolic, with the art bending at the seam.

prior_record.claim: REGISTRATION (measured): the canon art and the cityBox footprint differ in scale by roughly 10-16x. Consequence: no similarity or affine transform can make the art's coast or river land on the atlas's coast or river at both true scale and display scale. Registration has to choose. (a) Exaggerated inset: keep the enlarged city and rubber-sheet its rim to meet the atlas coast, roads and river at the crossfade ring (a TPS with GCPs on the seam). (b) True scale: the city shrinks to 2-3 atlas px and the zoom-through must bridge the gap.

items.summary: A GCP transform (Helmert/affine; @allmaps/transform documents the API) can warp vector geometry per vertex; implement it as a dependency-free offline tools/ script producing committed atlas-px JSON.

prior_record.claim: Vector geometry can be warped from art px into the atlas frame per vertex with a GCP transform. @allmaps/transform implements Helmert (2 GCPs), polynomial (3/6/10) and thin-plate spline (3 GCPs, exact at GCPs) on GeoJSON points, lines and polygons, forward and backward. It optionally adds midpoints so lines stay smooth under non-linear warps. A raster needs resampling or a WebGL warp. A vector needs only the transform applied to each vertex, offline or once at load.
prior_record.applies_to_us_proposed: Yes. Best used as an offline tool (node, in tools/) whose output is committed atlas-px JSON. A Helmert or TPS solve is also small enough to inline in vanilla JS if a runtime warp were wanted. GCP candidates in both frames: Summarch's two river crossings and four road exits, and Epēshu's coastline bends and the Road that Walks with the Sun exit (#15), matched to the atlas mask and dotted roads. Epēshu's off-city landmarks (Mount Mastery, Bangeph Rock, Fairy Arch) exist only in chart-pois.json (art px). They have no atlas-px marker, so they cannot be GCPs yet.

evidence.quote: transform[s] Points, LineStrings, Polygons and other spatial features from a 2D cartesian `(x, y)` source space to a destination space.
Thin Plate Spline | 3 | Smooth transformation; "exact" at GCPs
Default behavior applies no refinement (`maxDepth = 0`).

votes.corrected: The README (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/allmaps/allmaps/main/packages/transform/README.md, fetched OK) supports this much. @allmaps/transform builds a transformation from control points (GCPs) and applies it to Points, LineStrings, Polygons and other spatial features, from a 2D cartesian source space to a destination space. It transforms in both directions (GeneralGcpTransformer.transformForward/transformBackward). The minimum GCP counts are: helmert 2, polynomial 3, polynomial2 6, polynomial3 10, thinPlateSpline 3. The thinPlateSpline row says "Applies smooth transformation. Transformation is 'exact' at GPCs." For lines and polygons the transform can recursively add midpoints (maxDepth, minSourceDistance, minDestinationDistance, minOffsetRatio, minOffsetDistance) to keep results granular under non-shape-preserving warps. Refinement is off by default ("By default, `maxDepth = 0` and no refinement is applied."). The package's own types are Geometries, not GeoJSON. GeoJSON works only after conversion with geojsonGeometryToGeometry / geometryToGeojsonGeometry from @allmaps/stdlib. The raster-versus-vector comparison ("a raster needs resampling or WebGL; a vector needs only a per-vertex transform, offline or once at load") is the researcher's inference. The README never states it, apart from mentioning a WebGL2Renderer for rendering warped maps. Keep it as an engineering judgement, not as a sourced fact. The "applies_to_us" part is also unsourced from this README. I found "Mount Mastery", "Bangeph Rock" and "Fairy Arch" in maps-site/data/chart-pois.json. The rest (GCP candidates, no atlas-px markers) was not checked in this pass.

Quote 1 matches the README apart from the bold markers and the "[s]" edit. items.summary: QGIS's TPS suits deformed maps but needs ~10+ GCPs, while an Epēshu box holds only ~3-6 identifiable features, so TPS does not fit; QGIS is at most an offline aid for picking points.

prior_record.claim: Desktop GIS uses the same rubber-sheet registration for distorted hand-made maps. The QGIS Georeferencer's thin-plate spline fits multiple local polynomials to the GCPs and is meant for deformed or inaccurate maps. It needs about 10 or more GCPs.
prior_record.applies_to_us_proposed: Partly. QGIS is a good offline tool for picking GCPs by hand against the z5 tiles (no y-flip, atlas px = z5 px / 2), but nothing ships. Our seam fit needs few GCPs and should stay in a node tool or a JSON GCP list, not in a QGIS project.

evidence.quote: TPS is most useful for georeferencing damaged, deformed, or otherwise slightly inaccurate maps
It technically requires a minimum of 10 GCPs, but usually more to be successful.

Inside that box the atlas shows roughly 3 to 6 features you can identify: a coast or harbor point, a river mouth, and the points where the dotted roads leave the city. That is too few for TPS, which would overfit or fold. The fit we need is a similarity or affine transform from 3 to 4 GCPs, solved by least squares, which bends the DM art onto the atlas. QGIS is acceptable as a UI for clicking those GCPs. Pick them on PatrinorModern.png at native atlas px, or on the stitched z5 tiles, where atlas px = z5 px / 2 and there is no y-flip. Watch one trap when converting: QGIS .points files store the source pixel Y as negative (y-up) for ungeoreferenced rasters. Convert the points into a committed JSON list, for example a gcps field per city in city-anchors.json. A small node tool then solves the transform, and the atlas applies it in place of the cityBox box fit. Do not ship a QGIS project or a QGIS-warped GeoTIFF or JPG. The warp belongs in our own data, and the chart pyramids must stay consistent with it. This is a registration fix; it does not change the rendering medium. A vector city would need the same GCP transform. Anything that touches genCityCanvas, sampleCityMask or washMake must go through the mobile pins (UG3 atlas_fn_sha, cityCanvasSha).
votes.reason: The factual claim holds. The QGIS docs describe TPS as being for deformed maps, with a minimum of about 10 GCPs. The applies_to_us text is mostly right: QGIS should not ship and the GCPs should live in JSON or a node tool. But it is internally inconsistent. It says our seam fit needs few GCPs, which is true, yet it brings in a method whose defining requirement is 10 or more. I checked in the HEAD copy: cityBox(a,w,h) centres a box of radius footR(kind) on atlasX/atlasY (capital 26, town 14 world px). That is too small to supply 10 well-spread GCPs, so the right method for us is a few-point similarity or affine fit, not TPS. The QGIS part only helps as a point-picking tool, and its .points files flip the sign of Y, which our conversion has to undo. The correction states this, keeps registration separate from the rendering medium, and keeps the atlas authoritative (the art is bent to the atlas, never the reverse).

items.summary: Potrace (GPL) traces bitmaps to SVG/GeoJSON with a cutoff and mkbitmap pre-processing, AutoTrace adds centerline mode; both are offline-only tools whose output is committed data, and per-class masking is our inference.

prior_record.claim: Potrace traces only binary bitmaps. It outputs SVG and also GeoJSON, and colour art needs per-class pre-thresholding (mkbitmap). AutoTrace adds colour reduction and a centerline mode. Both are GPL (libautotrace is LGPL).
prior_record.applies_to_us_proposed: Yes, as offline tools only (GPL binaries are never shipped). Classify each colour class into a mask, then potrace each mask to GeoJSON in art px and warp it. AutoTrace -centerline (or a skeletonize step) gives road centerlines. Its centerline quality on our thin white roads is untested.

evidence.quote: produce the following output formats: SVG, PDF, EPS, PostScript, DXF, GeoJSON, PGM
Mkbitmap ... can be used to pre-process the input for better tracing behavior on greyscale and color images.
Outline and centerline tracing - trace the edges or centerlines of shapes

votes.corrected: Potrace (GPL) traces a bitmap into smooth vector paths. It outputs SVG, PDF, EPS, PostScript, DXF, GeoJSON, PGM, Gimppath and XFig. It accepts PBM, PGM, PPM or BMP input and reduces grey or colour input to black/white with a cutoff (-k/--blacklevel, default 0.5). Its bundled mkbitmap tool can "pre-process the input for better tracing behavior on greyscale and color images". Separating colour art into per-class masks before running potrace is our own workflow, not something potrace or mkbitmap does. AutoTrace (GPL v2 or later; libautotrace LGPL v2.1 or later) offers outline and centerline tracing and colour reduction (README examples: -centerline and -color-count 4). Whether AutoTrace's centerline mode works on our thin white roads is untested.
votes.reason: I fetched potrace.sourceforge.net and the AutoTrace README on 2026-10-07. Three quotes check out: the potrace output-format list including GeoJSON, the mkbitmap pre-processing sentence, and the AutoTrace "Outline and centerline tracing" line. The AutoTrace licence split (GPL v2 or later, LGPL v2.1 or later for libautotrace) is in its README. Potrace is GPL per its licence section. Colour reduction and the -centerline option are in the AutoTrace README. Two parts overreach. (1) "Potrace traces only binary bitmaps" is imprecise: the page says input may be PBM, PGM, PPM or BMP, and potrace itself thresholds grey and colour input with -k/--blacklevel. Only the tracing core works on a black/white bitmap. (2) "colour art needs per-class pre-thresholding (mkbitmap)" is not in the source. The page says only that mkbitmap helps on greyscale and colour images. Per-class colour masks would be our own preprocessing, not mkbitmap, which works on greyscale. The proposed pipeline is plausible but is not backed by the quotes.

votes.corrected:
Yes, but only as an offline, owner-run preprocessing step, and it is a medium step, not the alignment fix. Potrace and AutoTrace are never shipped or ported into maps-site/index.html; the npm potrace port is also GPL-2. The step would be a tools/ node script, like tools/build-gazetteer.js, that writes committed, deterministic data under maps-site/data/. Neither binary is installed in this environment.

Pipeline: denoise the JPEG art first (median filter plus colour quantization or mkbitmap), because overlay-Epeshu.jpg is a baseline JPEG and per-class thresholds on it give speckle. Then run potrace per mask with -b geojson, turdsize and opttolerance set, and simplify further to fit the mobile per-frame vertex budget.

Gotchas:
- Potrace coordinates use a bottom-left origin in art px. Flip y before applying any art-to-atlas transform, because the atlas has no y-flip.
- Classes traced independently do not share boundaries, so adjacent blocks, streets and water gap or overlap. Shared vertices need a planar or topological pass, for example a label-image polygonization.
- AutoTrace centerlines, or a skeleton, give unnoded polylines with spurs. Junction snapping and graph cleanup are needed before they can be roads. Quality on the thin white roads is untested.

Alignment comes only from the warp, which is a control-point registration of art features to atlas coast, river and road. Placing the traced GeoJSON through cityBox misaligns exactly as the raster does.

Any vector city layer falls inside filigree slice C ("painted city, pooled edges") and must obey R4 (no block labels) and R7 (nothing at rest; halos on hover only). It must not touch the hash-pinned genCityCanvas, washMake and sampleCityMask.
votes.reason:
The tool facts are correct. Potrace traces only bitmaps and has SVG, PDF, EPS, DXF, GeoJSON and PGM backends. mkbitmap is its pre-processor. AutoTrace has colour reduction and a centerline mode. The AutoTrace program is GPL and libautotrace is LGPL. "Offline only, never shipped" is the right fit for a single-file, no-build app.

The claim's applies_to_us undersells several issues that matter here:
- Registration: it says "potrace each mask ... and warp it" without saying that the warp is the whole alignment fix. Tracing changes the medium, not the registration, so a traced city placed through cityBox (FOOT_R in maps-site/index.html) shifts just as the image overlay does.
- Y origin: potrace output has a bottom-left origin, but the atlas mapping has no y-flip, so the y axis must be flipped first.
- JPEG noise: the DM overlays are JPEGs (overlay-Epeshu.jpg is baseline JPEG, 2863x3072, so the brief's "3072x2863" swaps the dimensions). Thresholding them per class needs denoising first.
- Shared edges: masks traced separately do not share edges. That defeats the "shared road vertices" benefit unless a topology pass follows.
- Vertex budget: raw traces are too heavy for the mobile per-frame budget without simplification.
- Determinism: the output must be committed, generated data from a tools/ script, which keeps the seeded world unaffected.
- Ownership: this work belongs to filigree slice C, which owns the painted city in docs/filigree/README.md. Rulings R4 and R7 apply. The pinned genCityCanvas, washMake and sampleCityMask must stay untouched.
- Availability: neither potrace nor autotrace is installed here.

These are refinements rather than a reversal, so the claim holds with a corrected applies_to_us.

items.summary: VTracer's colour pipeline and compact stacked output are in its README, but the other stated details were not supported, and tracing does not fix drift.

prior_record.claim: VTracer traces colour images directly with hierarchical clustering and spline fitting. Its stacked output is more compact than Illustrator Image Trace. It ships an npm WebAssembly build with no native dependency, under the MIT licence. Stacked shapes overlap, though, and carry no semantic class.
prior_record.applies_to_us_proposed: Partly. Its MIT licence and wasm build make it the easiest tracer for a node tool. Stacked output is good for a look-alike repaint. It is bad for interactivity, because a building is not a polygon of its own and roads are not a graph. Prefer per-class masks plus potrace or contours for footprints.

evidence.quote: skips Potrace's expensive optimal-polygon search in favor of a fast, linear pipeline that stays faithful to high-resolution images
VTracer's output is much more compact as we adopt a stacking strategy and avoid producing shapes with holes
VTracer is available as a Node.js WebAssembly build with "no native dependency,"

votes.corrected: VTracer (visioncortex) converts raster images, including coloured ones, to SVG through a colour-clustering pipeline with spline curve fitting (README: "Comparing to Potrace, VTracer has an image processing pipeline which can handle colored images ... a fast, linear pipeline"; flags `--hierarchical stacked|cutout`, `--mode pixel|polygon|spline`). The README says its output is "much more compact" than Illustrator Image Trace because it uses stacking and avoids shapes with holes. That is the vendor's own unbenchmarked comparison. The npm package @visioncortex/vtracer is a Node.js WebAssembly build with "no native dependency", but its latest version is 1.0.0-alpha.4. The licence is dual "MIT OR Apache-2.0" (Cargo.toml, nodejs/package.json, npm metadata), not MIT alone. The README quotes never mention the licence. The README does not state that stacked shapes overlap or have no semantic class. Those are the researcher's inference, which is plausible because stacking layers shapes on top of each other and the output is an unlabelled colour trace. The 1.0 README also documents `--hierarchical cutout`, a gapless mosaic with shared boundaries, so overlap is a default mode and not a fixed property. The github.com page could not be fetched in this environment (proxy blocked it), but raw.githubusercontent.com README, LICENSE, Cargo.toml and nodejs files were read and carry the same text.
votes.reason: The core facts check out against the raw README: the Potrace and Illustrator comparison sentences exist, and so does the Node WebAssembly "no native dependency" line. Four parts of the claim overreach. (1) The cited github.com URL was unreachable, though the raw README has the same text. (2) "Under the MIT licence" is incomplete, because the licence is "MIT OR Apache-2.0" and no cited quote covers licensing. (3) "Stacked shapes overlap, though, and carry no semantic class" is uncited inference, and the README now offers a seam-free cutout mode that shares boundaries. (4) "More compact than Illustrator" is the vendor's own assertion, and the npm build is only an alpha (1.0.0-alpha.4). The "traces colour images directly" and "no native dependency" parts hold. The applies_to_us conclusion (per-class masks plus potrace or contours for footprints) is judgement, not evidence, and is not weakened by these corrections.

votes.corrected: Partly, and only as an offline authoring aid. It does not fix the drift. REGISTRATION: a VTracer SVG of overlay-Epeshu.jpg or overlay-Summarch.jpg placed through cityBox(a,w,h), which is a FOOT_R box centred on the anchor, is off by exactly as much as the raster. Tracing changes the RENDERING MEDIUM, not the registration. First warp the source art to atlas control points (coast, river mouths, road ends) and then trace. The atlas stays authoritative, and the DM art stays canon as the reference layer, not something to replace. MEDIUM: the default `stacked` mode gives overlapping colour blobs. The current README also offers `--hierarchical cutout`, a seam-free mosaic with no overlap, so overlap is not the real blocker. Neither mode yields semantic classes, separate building polygons or a road graph. So it cannot drive per-building hover halos (R7) or shared road vertices on its own. Use it at most for a look-alike repaint inside filigree slice C. TOOLING: the npm package `@visioncortex/vtracer` is wasm with no native dependency, but it is a prerelease (1.0.0-alpha.4). The repo has no package.json, and every script in tools/ uses Node built-ins only, so adding it would be the first third-party dependency. Pin the version and commit the generated output. It should never ship to the page, which keeps it off the mobile frame budget and away from the sha pins on genCityCanvas, sampleCityMask and cityCanvasSha. For footprints, prefer per-class colour masks plus a small self-written contour tracer (marching squares with simplification) in tools/, rather than potrace. Potrace is GPL, so it is not a drop-in for an MIT project.
votes.reason: The facts mostly check out. The README says the output is "much more compact" than Illustrator Image Trace because of stacking and no holes. The `@visioncortex/vtracer` package is a "Node.js WebAssembly build, no native dependency", and the licence is MIT. The claim is out of date in one place: the CLI now has `--hierarchical cutout` ("seam-free mosaic"), so overlap is only the default behaviour. applies_to_us is too generous, though. It never says that tracing is a change of rendering medium and does nothing for registration, which is the owner's actual problem. In maps-site/index.html, cityBox sizes the overlay from FOOT_R[kind] around the anchor dot whatever the image shows, so a traced SVG would drift the same way. It also leaves out four costs. The npm release is still alpha. It would be the first non-built-in dependency, since tools/*.js require only fs, path, crypto, zlib, os, http, net and child_process. Potrace, which it recommends, is GPL. Any city vector look belongs to filigree slice C (R4, R7). Acting on it as a fix for alignment would be wrong. As an offline repaint aid, run after the art has been warped to atlas control points, it is acceptable.

items.summary: Both canon charts are flat-colour digital art; a simple colour rule with 4-connected labelling finds 17,323 Epēshu blobs ≥12 px (2,793 ≥40) and 3,769 in Summarch on the overlay JPGs.

prior_record.claim: Measured: both canon city maps are flat-colour digital art, not scans, so classes can be separated by simple colour rules. A building rule (R-G>18, G-B>18, 150<R<235) plus connected components finds about 17,323 building blobs of 12 px or more in Epēshu (2,793 of 40 px or more) and about 3,769 in Summarch (3,682 of 40 px or more). The water rule covers about 16.7% of Epēshu's pixels. Dark outlines already split touching buildings.
prior_record.applies_to_us_proposed: Yes. Segmenting by colour plus watershed or connected components is enough, with no ML or GPU. The counts are rough (JPEG fringes, badge and legend occlusion, uncalibrated thresholds) but put Epēshu at about 10^4 footprints and Summarch at a few thousand. Those counts drive both effort and render budget.

evidence.quote: Epeshu bldg px 6.1% components>=12px 17323 >=40px 2793 water px 16.7%
Summarch bldg px 9.7% components>=12px 3769 >=40px 3682 water px 2.4%

votes.corrected: Reproduced from the HEAD copies of maps-site/art/overlay-Epeshu.jpg (2863x3072) and overlay-Summarch.jpg (3072x2859). The building rule (R-G>18, G-B>18, 150<R<235) with 4-connected scipy.ndimage.label gives Epēshu 6.1% building pixels, 17,323 components of 12 px or more, 2,793 of 40 px or more. Summarch gives 9.7%, 3,769 and 3,682. These match the quoted figures exactly. 8-connectivity gives 17,723/2,864 for Epēshu, so the counts depend on the connectivity choice. Narrow wording: both maps are flat-fill digital art (about 3k and 2k colours at 5-bit quantization, with JPEG fringes), and the dark outlines visibly separate touching buildings in the mask overlays. A simple colour rule plus connected components segments building fills without ML. Caveats: (1) The Epēshu water 16.7% is not tied to a stated rule. A blue-over-red rule (B-R>15) gives 16.8% and a teal rule gives 15.9%. The Summarch water 2.4% in the evidence quote was not reproduced (1.6-1.8% with my rules), and the claim text does not cite it. (2) Epēshu blobs are tiny: the median is 24 px, the 99th percentile is 69 px and the maximum is 118 px. About 14.5k of the 17.3k blobs are under 40 px, so "about 10^4 footprints" holds only as colour-blob candidates (sheds, fragments, fringe pixels), and the 2,793 blobs of 40 px or more are the safer count of resolvable buildings. (3) Summarch blobs are much larger (median 202 px, maximum 4,536 px), so some touching buildings there may merge.
votes.reason: I reran the stated rule and reproduced both sets of quoted building counts and percentages exactly, using 4-connected labelling. The colour-rule claim is supported, and visual mask overlays confirm the images are flat-fill digital art with outlines separating buildings. Gaps: the water rule is unspecified and gives about 16-17% for Epēshu, but the 2.4% for Summarch was not reproduced. The Epēshu 17k figure is dominated by tiny blobs under 40 px, so it overstates resolvable building footprints.

votes.corrected: Yes, as an offline measurement and feasibility input, not as an alignment fix. I re-ran the stated rule on the HEAD files and got the same numbers. Epēshu: 6.1% building pixels, 17,323 blobs of 12 px or more, 2,793 of 40 px or more, largest blob 118 px, none of 200 px or more. Summarch: 9.7% building pixels, 3,769 and 3,682 blobs, 1,911 of 200 px or more, largest 4,536 px (The Seat compound, merged around badge 5). Both images are flat-colour vector-style art, so colour rules plus connected components are enough, with no ML or GPU. Caveats: (1) The mask leaves out the JPEG fringe and the dark outline, so each blob is 1 to 2 px smaller than the drawn building. Footprints need a dilation of about the outline width before they become polygons. (2) In Epēshu 84% of blobs are 12 to 40 px houses at 3072 px across, so about 10^4 is real but tiny. Some big buildings may be drawn in a different colour and missed (largest match is 118 px), so landmarks need their own colour rules or hand marking. The numbered badges (19 in Epēshu, 9 in Summarch) and the legend boxes hide or merge buildings. (3) Extraction has to be a deterministic offline tool that emits committed JSON, in the style of tools/build-gazetteer.js and preferably in node. It must not run in the page. It must not change the hash-pinned genCityCanvas, sampleCityMask or washMake. (4) The polygons come out in image pixel coordinates. Placed through cityBox they misalign exactly as the raster does today. Registration means fitting a transform that bends the art to the atlas coast, rivers and roads. That is a separate step, and it is the one that fixes the drift. Summarch's 0-250-500 scale bar can help fit its scale. (5) Render budget: about 17k Epēshu polygons is too many for a per-frame Leaflet SVG on mobile. Use the canvas renderer or pre-baked tiles, simplify the shapes, and show them only at deep zoom. How it is drawn belongs to filigree slice C (painted city, pooled edges; R4 no block labels; R7 halos on hover only).
votes.reason: I reproduced the measurement exactly with numpy/scipy on HEAD maps-site/art/overlay-Epeshu.jpg and overlay-Summarch.jpg. I also checked masked crops by eye: the rule fills building interiors, and dark outlines do split neighbouring houses. Summarch's largest blob is The Seat compound wrapped around badge 5. So the claim is right that this is feasible and right about the order of magnitude, and acting on it as a planning input is sound. applies_to_us needed qualifying in three ways. First, the extracted vectors sit in image space and do nothing for registration on their own. A vector city placed through cityBox drifts just as the raster does, so the alignment fix is a separate step that warps the art onto the atlas. Second, the counts are of shrunken interiors, and the large or landmark buildings may be missed, so the counts are not finished footprints. Third, the work has to stay an offline deterministic tool producing committed data, clear of the pinned functions and the mobile lane, with rendering left to the filigree city slice and kept within the mobile budget through a canvas or tile renderer.

items.summary: The deep-learning historical-atlas vectorization pipeline (PyTorch, CUDA) solves noisy scans and is overkill for our clean charts; keep at most classical watershed as optional offline tooling.

prior_record.claim: The peer-reviewed vectorization pipeline for historical city atlases is a supervised deep edge filter followed by watershed closed-shape extraction. It was trained on annotated 19th-century Paris atlas tiles and needs PyTorch on a CUDA GPU. Our digest records that U-Nets generalized better than transformers and that classical Meyer watershed beat the learned one.
prior_record.applies_to_us_proposed: No, as a whole pipeline. It solves noisy scanned maps, and our art is clean and flat-coloured (V8). Keep only the classical Meyer watershed idea for splitting merged footprints. No training data, GPU or Python stack is needed.

evidence.quote: edge filtering using deep learning models, closed shape extraction via watershed transform, and raster-to-vector conversion
U-Net-family edge filtering → **classical Meyer watershed** for closed-shape extraction — U-Nets generalized better than transformer edge detectors
a supervised pipeline designed to reliably extract closed shapes from historical maps, specifically from Paris atlases

votes.corrected: The soduco Benchmark_historical_map_vectorization repo (README, fetched via raw.githubusercontent.com) describes a Paris-atlas pipeline (atlases from the 19th and early 20th centuries) with three stages: deep edge filtering, watershed closed-shape extraction, and raster-to-vector conversion. It compares deep edge detectors, including vision transformers, and several deep and classical watershed approaches. The code is PyTorch, and its training and inference commands pass a --cuda --gpu flag. The "needs a CUDA GPU" wording is not supported: --cuda is a command-line flag, and the README never says CPU is unsupported. Our digest (docs/research/accurate-mapping.md, "Two-stage pipeline for scanned maps") does record "U-Net-family edge filtering → classical Meyer watershed ... U-Nets generalized better than transformer edge detectors, and the classical watershed beat the end-to-end deep one". That is a record of what the digest says. It is not independently confirmed by the README, which names the watershed, Meyer-watershed and transformer comparisons only as things the benchmark covers. The README does not say "peer-reviewed", "supervised" or "trained on annotated tiles". The PLOS ONE paper (cited as the source of the peer-review and "supervised" wording) could not be reached: the repec snippet fetch returned a proxy 403.
votes.reason: The core description holds: deep edge filter, then watershed, then vectorization, on Paris atlases, with the digest quote present. Four points fail or overreach. (1) The quoted GitHub sentence is a paraphrase, not verbatim; the README reads "edge filtering stage using deep filters, a closed shape extraction stage using a watershed transform, and a raster-to-vector conversion stage". (2) The PLOS/repec "supervised ... closed shapes" source was unreachable (403), so the quote, "peer-reviewed" and "supervised" could not be verified. (3) "Needs PyTorch on a CUDA GPU" overreaches: the README shows PyTorch models and a --cuda flag but does not state that a GPU is required, and the inference script path returned 404. (4) "19th-century" is narrower than the README's "19th and early 20th centuries", and "annotated tiles" is only implied by the dataset and ground-truth download. The applies_to_us conclusion is a judgement call, not a sourced claim, and is not affected.

votes.corrected: No, as a whole pipeline: it was trained to clean noisy scans of 19th-century Paris atlases and needs PyTorch on a CUDA GPU. Our two canon city images (maps-site/art/overlay-Epeshu.jpg and overlay-Summarch.jpg) are already clean flat colour: tan building blocks with dark outlines, green tree clumps, cream ground, dark numeral badges. A deep edge filter has nothing to remove there. Keep only one part of it, and only as optional offline tooling run once. Threshold the building colour, mask out trees, badges and JPEG fringes, then use a distance-transform plus classical (Meyer) marker watershed to split footprints that share a wall. The output is committed, hand-checked polygon data in art pixel space. Nothing about it runs in the browser, so it does not touch the seeded generation, the mobile frame budget or the hash-pinned genCityCanvas, washMake and sampleCityMask. First ask the DM whether the vector source these maps were drawn from still exists; it would make tracing unnecessary. This is a choice of rendering medium only. Traced polygons placed through cityBox misalign exactly as the image does. Fixing alignment still needs separate registration: tie art points to atlas coast, river and road points and warp the art onto the atlas, never the atlas onto the art. Painted-city styling then belongs to the filigree slice C and follows R4/R7: no block labels, highlights on hover only.
votes.reason: The claim matches the soduco benchmark and docs/research/accurate-mapping.md, which records U-Net edge filtering, the classical Meyer watershed winning and Paris atlases. That doc also lists 'transfer to a single hand-drawn fantasy map' as an open question. I looked at 400px crops of both overlay JPGs. They are crisp, generator-style flat colour, so dropping the deep stage is right, and so is keeping watershed for footprints that share a wall. The 'V8' cross-reference could not be checked, but the crops confirm what it says. The verdict needs four additions. (1) It is offline tooling run once, and its committed output is data, so determinism, the pins and the per-frame budget are untouched. (2) Watershed needs markers from a distance transform, and the badges, trees and JPEG ringing must be masked first. (3) Asking the DM for the original vector export is cheaper than tracing. (4) The key distinction: vectorizing does not fix the misalignment the owner reported. That comes from the art being dropped into a fixed-radius box by cityBox (FOOT_R), so control-point registration to the atlas is still needed.

items.summary: mapKurator spots and OSM-links text on scanned historical maps; it does not apply, since Nīmlad has no OSM entities and the chart POIs are already in chart-pois.json.

prior_record.claim: mapKurator is an automatic pipeline that detects, OCRs and links text labels on large collections of scanned historical maps (the Rumsey set). It links places to OpenStreetMap entities and uses separate spotter models.
prior_record.applies_to_us_proposed: No. Our city maps carry numbered badges and a legend, and their 19 + 9 POIs are already in chart-pois.json. What the tracer actually needs is the reverse: mask the badges, legend panel and compass rose and in-fill under them before tracing. Filigree R4 (never label blocks) and R7 (nothing at rest, halos on hover only) mean the vector layer carries no visible text at rest anyway.

evidence.quote: a fully automatic pipeline developed by the Knowledge Computing Lab at the University of Minnesota to process a large number of scanned historical map images.
The mapKurator System: A Complete Pipeline for Extracting and Linking Text from Historical Maps

votes.corrected: mapKurator (Knowledge Computing Lab, University of Minnesota) is a fully automatic pipeline for scanned historical map images. Its outputs are recognized text labels, label bounding polygons, post-OCR-corrected labels and an OpenStreetMap geo-entity identifier. Its spotter models (Spotter-v2, PALETTE) sit in separate repositories. Its derived dataset covers English map text from the Rumsey collection (57K georeferenced maps).
votes.reason: The raw README fetched from raw.githubusercontent.com contains the first quote word for word, apart from bold and link markup. It describes mapKurator as "a fully automatic pipeline developed by the Knowledge Computing Lab at the University of Minnesota to process a large number of scanned historical map images." The second quote is the title in the README's BibTeX citation, "The mapKurator System: A Complete Pipeline for Extracting and Linking Text from Historical Maps". The README also supports the rest of the claim. Outputs include recognized text labels, label bounding polygons, post-OCR-corrected labels and an OpenStreetMap geo-entity identifier. It has a "mapKurator textspotter repository" section that lists the separate spotter models Spotter-v2 and PALETTE. Its data card says the text was recognized from the Rumsey collection of 57K georeferenced maps, and that dataset is English-only. I did not separately confirm the github.com page text, but the raw README matches. For applies_to_us, maps-site/data/chart-pois.json in the HEAD export has 19 Epēshu POIs and 9 Summarch POIs. docs/filigree/README.md lists R4 as "never label blocks" and R7 as "nothing at rest; halos stay hover-only". The claim is slightly loose in two ways. "Detects" is only implied by the label bounding polygons. The Rumsey processing is one derived dataset, not the only target.

votes.corrected: No, not as a pipeline to adopt. Text extraction is neither the registration fix (snapping art to atlas coast, rivers and roads) nor the rendering medium. mapKurator links places to OpenStreetMap entities, and Nīmlad has none. It is also a heavy Python/ML stack trained on the Rumsey corpus, which cannot sit in one vanilla, build-free file. The two DM city charts are already read by hand: maps-site/data/chart-pois.json holds Epēshu 19 and Summarch 9 numbered POIs in chart-image pixel space. The atlas settlement names are already covered by the wiki Leaflet markers and the gazetteer (tools/build-gazetteer.js). What the tracer actually needs is the reverse of label extraction: mask the numeral badges, the legend panel and the compass rose and in-fill under them before tracing, so they do not become false buildings or walls. chart-pois.json is the ground truth that says where each badge sits. Its x/y are in chart space, so they place the masks but are not atlas control points for registration. Filigree R4 forbids labels on blocks and allows only street/arterial names, and only past a zoom threshold inside the city band. R7 means nothing shows at rest and halos appear on hover only. So any text on the vector layer comes from our own data, never from OCR of the art. Keep mapKurator only as a footnote in docs/research/accurate-mapping.md, and drop that doc's framing that it fits our settlement-label sweeps over PatrinorModern.png.
votes.reason: The claim's description of mapKurator matches its README. The applies_to_us verdict of 'No' is correct for this stack. There is no OSM to link to in a fictional world. The ML/Python toolchain conflicts with one vanilla file, no build. There are only two hand-drawn charts, whose POIs are already transcribed in maps-site/data/chart-pois.json (verified: Epēshu 19, Summarch 9). And text extraction does nothing for registration, which is what fixes the owner's misalignment. The suggestion to mask badges, legend and compass and in-fill before tracing is sound. Two small corrections. First, R4 (docs/filigree/README.md rulings table) does allow street/arterial names past a zoom threshold in the city band, so 'no visible text at rest anyway' slightly overstates it. Text may appear, but it comes from our data, not OCR. Second, chart-pois coordinates are in chart-image space, so they can place the masks but cannot serve as atlas registration control points. docs/research/accurate-mapping.md also oversells mapKurator as 'the exact shape of our settlement-label sweeps', which this verdict should counter.

items.summary: The hand-digitizing effort figures were an unsourced estimate; the skeleton-only point is carried by G0-19/G0-20 and asking the DM for Watabou sources by V17.

prior_record.claim: Effort (my estimate): digitizing every building by hand is out. At about 10 s per footprint, Epēshu's roughly 17k buildings take about 48 h and Summarch's about 10 h. Hand digitizing pays off only for the primary skeleton: coastline, river, walls and gates, main roads, district outlines and fields, a few tens to low hundreds of features per city (hours in QGIS, Inkscape or geojson.io). Inkscape's Trace Bitmap is Potrace wrapped with brightness, edge and colour-quantization scans. geojson.io is a lightweight browser editor.
prior_record.applies_to_us_proposed: Yes. Hybrid split: hand-trace primaries and GCPs (the registration-critical parts), auto-trace footprints from colour classes. Fidelity to the DM's art stays near 1:1 for footprints and is exact where traced by hand. The per-footprint time is my estimate, not a sourced figure.

evidence.quote: Color Quantization ... will find edges where colors change, even at equal brightness and contrast.
a browser-based tool for creating and editing spatial data for your mapping projects.

votes.corrected: Effort (author's own estimate, unsourced): hand-digitizing every building is impractical, and hand digitizing is best kept to the primary skeleton (coastline, river, walls and gates, main roads, district outlines, fields), a few tens to low hundreds of features per city. Only the geojson.io part is source-backed: its README calls it "a browser-based tool for creating and editing spatial data for your mapping projects" and "a fast, simple editor for map data", so "lightweight" is a paraphrase. The Inkscape claim (Trace Bitmap is Potrace wrapped with brightness, edge and colour-quantization scans) could not be verified. The building counts (Epēshu about 17k, Summarch about 10k) and the 10 s per footprint rate are not in the repo or any source. The hour totals are also not internally consistent: 17k at 10 s is about 47 h, but 10 h for Summarch implies only about 3.6k buildings, while the 10k figure above is the building count I read the "Summarch about 10 h" total as being drawn from, which would give about 28 h at 10 s.
votes.reason: The inkscape.org tutorial and the other Inkscape mirrors I tried returned CONNECT 403 from the proxy or a 404, so the Color Quantization quote and the Potrace framing are unverified; the evidence entry itself says it is only a search snippet. The geojson.io README fetched fine and supports the quote, but not the word "lightweight". Grepping the repo docs found no support for the ~17k or ~10k building counts; the only count is a 1245-building figure for the sim's Epēshu realm (settlements=19 buildings=1245), unrelated to the hand-digitizing totals. The per-footprint time and the hour totals are the author's own estimate, and the Summarch total does not follow from the same rate. The overall effort conclusion is a reasonable estimate, but the claim as stated attributes unverified specifics to sources.

The effort arithmetic mostly holds. Hand-digitizing every footprint is out. My rough colour-component count on maps-site/art/overlay-Summarch.jpg found about 3.3k to 3.7k blobs of 20 px or more, which fits "about 10 h". Epēshu's 17k is unverified: my colour threshold failed on its JPG. It is plausible from the density of the art. Hand-tracing only the skeleton (coast, river, walls and gates, main roads, districts and fields) is the right split, and those features are exactly the registration evidence. But applies_to_us overstates in four ways.

(1) It misses the cheapest route. Both canon city maps are visibly Watabou Medieval Fantasy City Generator / City Generator output: flat fills, ward layout, walled towers, compass rose, numbered legend and scale bar on Sun's March, and the alley-grain style on Epēshu. That generator can export GeoJSON. If the DM still has the generator link/seed or the export, footprints, roads, walls and water come out as exact vectors, with no tracing at all. Ask the DM first. docs/research/town-generation.md lists Watabou internals as an open question, and no doc mentions export.

(2) "Fidelity near 1:1 for footprints" from colour classes is too strong for these files. They are JPEGs. In Epēshu, wall-sharing houses are split only by thin dark outlines, so a colour-class or Potrace trace will merge them into block blobs.
